events.after: Resources / Sheet / Deep Draw Stamping: Process, Materials, and Applications Deep Draw Stamping: Process, Materials, and Applications Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 27 min read Published July 2, 2026 Updated October 30, 2026 Deep draw stamping is a sheet metal forming process in which a flat metal blank is drawn into a die cavity by a punch to produce hollow, single components. The process produces parts with a depth greater than the diameter, covering cylindrical, box-shaped, and complex geometric forms. The materials used range from low-carbon steel and aluminum alloys to stainless steel and copper-based alloys, each selected for ductility and formability. The applications span automotive, aerospace, appliance, electronics, and industrial manufacturing sectors, where high-volume output and dimensional consistency are required. A single draw cycle transforms a flat blank into a net-shape hollow part without welding or joining, eliminating structural weak points found in fabricated assemblies. The process operates at production rates from 15 to 40 parts per minute on mechanical presses, supporting large-scale manufacturing programs with consistent dimensional repeatability. Limiting draw ratios from 1.8 to 2.3 defines the geometric boundaries achievable in a single press stroke, with multi-stage sequences extending the capability to draw ratios above 3.0. Manufacturers across precision-driven industries rely on deep draw stamping for its repeatable accuracy, minimal material waste, and capacity to produce structurally sound parts at scale. What Is Deep Draw Stamping? Deep draw stamping is a sheet metal forming operation where a punch applies compressive force to the center of a flat metal blank, inducing tensile and compressive stresses as it pulls the material into a die cavity to produce a hollow part. The term "deep draw" refers specifically to parts in which the depth of the formed cavity exceeds the diameter of the punch, distinguishing it from shallow-draw forming processes. The punch descends into the die, pulling the surrounding material radially inward and downward, causing permanent plastic deformation without fracture. A draw ratio, calculated as blank diameter divided by punch diameter, quantifies the severity of the forming operation, with typical limiting draw ratios ranging from 1.8 to 2.3 for a single draw. Parts produced through deep draw stamping (canisters, enclosures, cups, and shells) are used across precision manufacturing industries. How Does Deep Draw Stamping Differ from Conventional Stamping? Deep draw stamping differs from conventional stamping through the depth and geometry of the deformation it produces in the metal blank. Conventional stamping performs cutting, blanking, piercing, or shallow bending operations, in which material displacement is minimal, and depth is limited. Deep drawing forces the blank through a die cavity using controlled radial and circumferential material flow, producing parts with substantial depth relative to the cross-sectional diameter. The blank holder in deep drawing exerts a controlled clamping force to prevent wrinkling, a requirement absent in standard stamping operations. The result is a structurally continuous, single hollow component that conventional stamping processes cannot replicate through a single-stage operation. Is Deep Draw Stamping Considered a Cold Forming Process? Yes, deep-draw stamping is considered a cold-forming process. The operation takes place at room temperature, where the metal blank undergoes plastic deformation without external heat. Cold forming preserves the metal's grain structure, producing parts with higher surface quality and tighter dimensional tolerances than hot forming. Work hardening occurs during cold drawing, increasing the tensile strength of the formed part by 10% to 30%, depending on the material and draw depth. Metals with high ductility and low yield strength (low-carbon steel and aluminum alloys) perform best under cold deep-draw stamping conditions. How Does the Deep Draw Stamping Process Work? The deep draw stamping process works by placing a pre-cut flat metal blank into an open-die cavity and securing it with a blank holder that applies controlled downward pressure. The punch then descends at a controlled rate, pushing the blank into the die cavity and initiating radial material flow from the blank flange region inward around the die entry radius, while the material directly beneath the punch face moves downward with negligible radial displacement. The metal stretches over the punch nose as the punch advances, compresses circumferentially at the flange, and deforms permanently into the shape of the die cavity. The punch stroke continues until the blank is drawn through the die opening or reaches a specified stroke depth, producing a hollow part with defined wall thickness, base geometry, and open top. Lubrication applied to the blank surface reduces friction at the die-metal interface, minimizing tool wear and preventing surface defects during the draw cycle. What Happens During Material Flow in Deep Drawing? A radially inward and axially downward movement of the sheet metal happens during the material flow in deep drawing. The blank flange region experiences compressive circumferential stress and tensile radial stress simultaneously as the punch descends, driving metal toward the die opening. The metal at the flange thickens slightly due to circumferential compression, while the metal at the punch nose wall thins due to tensile stretching. Thinning at the punch nose radius commonly ranges from 15% to 25% of the original blank thickness, depending on the draw ratio and material ductility. A strain gradient develops across the blank, with the highest thinning occurring near the punch radius, where biaxial tension is greatest. The forming limit curve (FLC) of the material defines the maximum permissible strain before localized necking initiates at the thinning zone. Controlling the blank holder force regulates the rate and direction of material flow, preventing wrinkling in the flange or tearing at the punch radius zone. Is Blank Holder Force Important in Deep Drawing? Yes, blank holder force is important in deep drawing. The force governs material flow behavior at the blank flange region throughout the entire punch stroke cycle. The circumferential compressive stresses in the flange cause the material to buckle without adequate blank holder force, producing wrinkles that compromise the structural integrity and surface quality of the formed part. Excessive blank holder force restricts material flow so severely that tensile stresses at the punch radius exceed the ultimate tensile strength of the material, causing tearing. The optimal blank holder pressure range is typically approximated based on 1.5% of the material's yield strength, which varies with material thickness, yield strength, die geometry, and draw ratio. Nitrogen gas springs or hydraulic cushions supply the blank-holder force in progressive and transfer die-stamping systems, delivering consistent clamping pressure across the full flange contact area. Precise blank-holder force control produces parts with uniform wall thickness, accurate geometry, and defect-free surfaces across high-volume deep-draw stamping production runs. What Materials Are Used in Deep Draw Stamping? The materials used in deep-draw stamping are metallic alloys selected for high ductility, sufficient elongation, and a controlled yield strength to withstand plastic deformation without fracture. The material must sustain substantial radial and circumferential stress during the forming cycle. Draw-grade metals with elongation values above 20% and low yield-to-tensile strength ratios (below 0.65) produce consistent part geometry across production runs. The materials used in deep-draw stamping are listed below. Low-Carbon Steel : Low-carbon steel (0.05% to 0.25% carbon content) exhibits elongation values from 30% to 45% and an r-value above 1.5, making it the predominant material for automotive panels, enclosures, and appliance housings. Stainless Steel : Stainless steel grades 304 and 316 offer corrosion resistance, elongation near 40%, and yield strength ranging from 215 MPa to 310 MPa, making the steel suitable for food-processing equipment, medical-device housings, and kitchen sinks. Aluminum Alloys : Aluminum alloys (1100, 3003, 5052) offer elongation of 20% to 35% and a density of 2.7 g/cm³, making the alloy preferable for aerospace and electronics enclosure applications that require weight reduction. Copper and Brass Alloys : Cartridge brass (C26000) achieves elongation exceeding 50% and a limiting draw ratio of 2.3, supporting electrical connectors, ammunition casings, and plumbing components without intermediate annealing during multi-stage reductions. Nickel Alloys : Nickel alloys (Inconel 625, Alloy 200) require intermediate annealing from 760°C to 1,040°C due to high work-hardening rates, and are used in aerospace fuel system components and chemical processing housings. Titanium Alloys : Commercially pure titanium (Grades 1 and 2) can be cold drawn at room temperature for moderate depths, but requires warm drawing at 200°C to 300°C for aggressive draw ratios to improve formability, with applications in medical implants, aerospace airframe components, and defense hardware. Why Are Good Material Properties Important for Deep Drawing? Good material properties are important for deep drawing because the severity of plastic deformation during the process demands that the blank sustain large strains without fracture. Ductility determines how far the material deforms before failure, with deep draw-grade steels requiring elongation above 30% to accommodate the required strain levels. The normal anisotropy ratio (r-value) quantifies a material's resistance to thinning in the thickness direction relative to in-plane deformation, with values above 1.6 indicating superior deep-drawability. Yield strength directly governs the blank holder force and punch load required to initiate and sustain material flow, affecting press capacity selection and tooling pattern. A material with balanced ductility, low yield-to-tensile strength ratio (below 0.65), and high uniform elongation produces consistent part geometry and minimizes the risk of tearing or wrinkling during deep-draw stamping. Are Ductile Metals Better for Deep Draw Stamping? Yes, ductile metals are better for deep draw stamping. Ductility allows the metal blank to undergo large plastic strains during forming without crack initiation or propagation at the punch radius or die entry zones. Metals with high elongation values (above 30%) and low yield-to-tensile strength ratios (below 0.65) flow uniformly into the die cavity, producing parts with consistent wall thickness and accurate geometry. The ductile metals used in deep draw stamping are low-carbon steel, copper alloys, and aluminum series 1100 and 300, with limiting draw ratios ranging from 1.8 to 2.3 in a single operation. Brittle metals fracture under the circumferential and radial stresses present during drawing, making brittle metals incompatible with the deep-draw stamping process. What Equipment Is Used in Deep Draw Stamping? The equipment used in deep draw stamping is a coordinated set of tooling and press systems created to apply controlled force, constrain material flow, and shape metal blanks into finished hollow parts. Press type, tooling geometry, and auxiliary systems determine the accuracy, cycle speed, and surface quality of the drawn component. Equipment selection directly affects draw ratio capability, dimensional repeatability, and production throughput across high-volume manufacturing programs. The equipment used in deep draw stamping is listed below. Punches : The punch is the male tooling component manufactured from tool steel grades (D2, H13) hardened to 58 to 62 Hardness Rockwell C-scale (HRC), with the punch radius and surface finish directly controlling the distribution of thinning and surface quality in the formed part. Dies : The die is the female tooling component fabricated from carbide or hardened tool steel, with a die entry radius from 4 to 10 times the material thickness, controlling material flow rate and stress concentration at the drawing edge. Blank Holders : The blank holder clamps the outer flange against the die face, applying an optimal holding pressure typically approximated at 1.5% of the material's yield strength to prevent wrinkling without restricting flow to the point of tearing. Hydraulic Presses : Hydraulic presses deliver constant force throughout the full punch stroke, with capacities ranging from 20 tons to over 2,000 tons, and adjustable stroke speed to optimize material flow behavior at different stages of the draw cycle. Mechanical Presses : Mechanical presses operate via a flywheel-and-crankshaft mechanism at stroke speeds of 15 to 40 strokes per minute, paired with progressive dies to produce deep-drawn parts reliably without tearing. Lubrication Systems : Automated spray, roller, or flood lubrication systems apply mineral oil-based, synthetic, or soap-based lubricants, reducing the coefficient of friction from 0.15 to 0.05 and lowering punch load requirements by a maximum of 30%. If you do not design around the limiting draw ratio early on (keeping punch radii generous and planning for realistic clearances to handle flange thickening), you are setting the toolroom up for splitting and wrinkling headaches. Ultimately, optimizing for high-volume stamping means respecting the material's yield strength and giving the metal the exact physical room it needs to displace cleanly into the die cavity." Audrius Zidonis PhD Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering How Do Punches and Dies Shape the Metal Blank? The punches and dies shape the metal blank through a coordinated mechanical action where the punch applies downward force, pressing the flat blank through the die opening and into the die cavity. The punch nose geometry defines the internal profile of the drawn part, while the die cavity geometry controls the external dimensions and wall angle of the finished component. The blank bends over the die entry radius as the punch descends, stretches along the punch nose, and flows radially inward from the flange region, conforming permanently to the tool geometry. Die clearance, set with an additional 10% to 20% of the material thickness over nominal gauge (110% to 120% of sheet thickness), controls wall-thickness uniformity and surface contact pressure during the draw stroke. The punch radius, die entry radius, and surface finish of both tools collectively determine the distribution of thinning, dimensional accuracy, and surface quality across the formed part. Does Proper Fluid Mechanics Improve Deep Drawing Performance? Yes, proper fluid mechanics improves deep-drawing performance. The behavior of forming lubricants at the blank-die and blank-punch interfaces follows fluid-mechanics principles, in which viscosity, pressure distribution, and film thickness govern friction reduction in contact zones. A hydrodynamic lubricant film with viscosity from 100 to 1,000 cSt separates the metal blank from the die surface, reducing the coefficient of friction from 0.15 to as low as 0.05 at the drawing edge. The reduction in interfacial friction lowers punch load requirements by a maximum of 30%, decreasing the risk of tearing at the punch nose radius zone during the draw stroke. Pressure-viscosity relationships at the die entry zone determine lubricant film stability under the compressive loads generated during drawing, making the understanding of fluid mechanics a foundational requirement for optimizing the lubrication system pattern in deep draw stamping. What Are the Design Considerations in Deep Draw Stamping? The design considerations in deep-draw stamping are geometric, material, and process parameters that engineers define before tooling fabrication to ensure part manufacturability and dimensional accuracy. Addressing the considerations during the pattern phase prevents tooling rework, elevated scrap rates, and extended development lead times. Draw ratio, corner radii, wall thickness, tolerance requirements, springback control, and friction management collectively determine whether a part geometry is producible within a single draw operation or requires multi-stage processing. The design considerations in deep-draw stamping are listed below. Draw Ratio : The draw ratio, calculated as the blank diameter divided by the punch diameter, has a limiting draw ratio (LDR) of 1.8 to 2.3 for single-stage operations, with ratios above 3.0 requiring multi-stage progressive drawing sequences. Corner Radii : Punch nose radii below 4 times the material thickness concentrate tensile stress, increasing tearing risk, while die entry radii set from 4 to 8 times material thickness permit smooth material flow without wrinkling. Wall Thickness : Wall thickness in deep drawn parts is non-uniform, with thinning at the punch nose radius reaching 15% to 25% of original blank thickness and flange regions thickening by 5% to 10%. Tolerance Requirements : Deep-draw stamping achieves tolerances of ±0.05 mm to ±0.25 mm, with tolerances below ±0.05 mm requiring ironing operations after the initial draw to ensure precise thickness control. Springback Control : Springback causes dimensional deviations of 0.5° to 5° after punch withdrawal, with high-yield-strength materials (above 350 MPa) requiring die-geometry compensation or ironing force at the final draw stage. Friction Management : The coefficient of friction at the die entry zone ranges from 0.05 to 0.15, controlled through tool surface coatings of Titanium Nitride (TiN) and Titanium Carbonitride (TiCN), and through die surface polishing to below 0.4 µm Ra to prevent friction-induced thinning and galling. How Does Draw Ratio Affect Manufacturability? The draw ratio affects manufacturability through its direct relationship to the radial tensile stress imposed on the blank material during the forming cycle. A draw ratio above the limiting draw ratio (LDR) of a given material generates tensile stresses at the punch radius that exceed the material's fracture strength, producing tears in the part wall. Low draw ratios (below 1.8) are achievable in a single press stroke without intermediate processing, minimizing tooling cost and cycle time. Draw ratios from 1.8 to 2.3 define the standard operable range for a single-stage deep draw, beyond which re-draw operations and intermediate annealing steps at temperatures from 650°C to 900°C become necessary. Engineers reduce effective draw ratios by increasing blank-holder force precision, optimizing die-entry radii, and selecting materials with high normal anisotropy (r-value above 1.6) to improve single-stage manufacturability. Can Excessive Draw Depth Cause Material Failure? Yes, excessive draw depth can cause material failure in deep-draw stamping. The tensile stress at the punch nose radius accumulates beyond the material's ultimate tensile strength as draw depth increases, initiating fracture at the weakest thinning zone of the part wall. The critical thinning zone near the punch radius experiences strain levels that exceed the material's forming limit curve (FLC), triggering localized necking and rupture. Draw depth-to-diameter ratios above 2.0 in a single pass without annealing or re-draw sequences consistently produce tearing in low-ductility materials with elongation values below 20%. Controlling draw depth through multi-stage drawing sequences, with intermediate anneals restoring elongation from 5% to 15% from stage to stage, prevents material failure in deep-part production. What Defects Occur in Deep Draw Stamping? The defects that occur in deep draw stamping are forming anomalies resulting from improper process parameters, tooling geometry errors, or inadequate material selection during the drawing operation. Identifying and correcting the defects at the process development stage reduces scrap rates and ensures dimensional conformity in production parts. The primary defect categories encountered in deep-draw stamping operations are wrinkling, tearing, earing, springback, surface galling, and thickness variation. The defects that occur in deep draw stamping are listed below. Wrinkling : Wrinkling is a buckling defect in the blank flange region caused by insufficient blank holder force. The wrinkling is corrected by increasing blank holder pressure by 10% to 20% and verifying parallelism with the die face. Tearing : Tearing is a fracture defect that initiates at the punch nose radius when tensile stress exceeds the material's ultimate tensile strength, and is corrected by reducing the draw ratio, increasing lubricant viscosity, and enlarging the punch nose radius. Earing : Earing is a scalloped edge defect at the open rim of a drawn cup caused by crystallographic planar anisotropy (Δr), reduced by maintaining planar anisotropy values below 0.2 and optimizing blank grain orientation. Springback : Springback is the elastic dimensional recovery after punch withdrawal, producing wall angle deviations of 0.5° to 5°, which are corrected through die geometry compensation or ironing operations at the final draw stage. Surface Galling : Surface galling is adhesive wear damage caused by metal-to-metal contact at die and punch interfaces, prevented by applying high-viscosity lubricants (100 to 1,000 cSt) and polishing die surfaces below Ra 0.4 µm. Thickness Variation : Thickness variation is a non-uniform wall-thickness distribution across the drawn part, with punch-nose thinning reaching 15% to 25%, reduced to within tight nominal tolerances through downstream ironing operations. What Causes Wrinkling During Deep Drawing? The insufficient blank-holder pressure, combined with excessive circumferential compressive stress in the flange region, causes wrinkling during deep drawing. The flange material flows radially inward and experiences compressive stress in the circumferential direction as the punch descends, perpendicular to the direction of material flow. The flange lacks sufficient restraint to prevent out-of-plane buckling, resulting in folds or waves in the drawn wall when the blank holder pressure falls below approximately 1.5% of the material's yield strength. Wrinkling severity increases with larger blank diameters, thinner material gauges (below 1.0 mm), and higher draw ratios, which amplify the magnitude of circumferential compressive stress. Corrective measures include increasing blank holder pressure by 10% to 20%, reducing the die entry radius to increase flow resistance, and selecting materials with higher planar stiffness to resist flange buckling during the draw stroke. Can Improper Tooling Cause Tearing Defects? Yes, improper tooling causes tearing defects in deep draw stamping. A punch radius below 4 times the material thickness concentrates tensile stress at the punch nose contact zone, reducing the material's ability to redistribute strain across the draw wall. Insufficient die entry radius (below 4 times material thickness) restricts material flow from the flange, increasing tensile load at the punch nose beyond the material's ultimate tensile strength. Tool surfaces with excessive roughness (above Ra 1.6 µm) increase friction at the blank-die interface, elevating punch load requirements and accelerating thinning at the critical strain zone. Hardened tooling maintained within the 58 to 62 HRC range, with precise punch-to-die clearance incorporating an additional 10% to 20% space above the nominal material thickness, prevents stress concentrations that initiate tearing defects in deep-draw stamping production. What Are the Advantages of Deep Draw Stamping? The advantages of deep draw stamping are process, quality, and economic benefits that make it the preferred forming method for high-volume hollow component production. The process delivers single-part geometry, high-dimensional repeatability, and streamlined material utilization within a single automated press cycle. A high production speed, excellent repeatability, single-part formation, reduced secondary assembly, streamlined material use, and good surface finish collectively define the manufacturing value of deep-draw stamping. The advantages of deep draw stamping are listed below. High Production Speed : Mechanical presses paired with progressive dies produce deep-draw parts at rates from 15 to 40 strokes per minute, with automated blank feeding sustaining continuous output across multi-shift operations at volumes exceeding 10,000 parts. Excellent Repeatability : Deep draw stamping delivers dimensional tolerances of ±0.05 mm to ±0.25 mm across millions of parts, with tool steel punches and dies hardened to 58 to 62 HRC, maintaining dimensional stability without measurable geometric drift. Seamless Part Formation : Deep-draw stamping produces hollow components without welding or secondary assembly, with a single draw cycle transforming a flat blank into a net-shape hollow part, ensuring continuous grain flow through the part wall. Reduced Secondary Assembly : Deep-draw parts exit the press as near-net-shape components, eliminating secondary operations and reducing total manufacturing lead time by 20% to 40% while lowering labor costs compared to fabricated-part alternatives. Streamlined Material Usage : Deep draw stamping achieves material utilization rates of 85% to 95% of the original blank area, with nesting that streamlines blank layouts on coil stock, further reducing scrap from inter-blank spacing during blanking operations. Good Surface Finish : Deep-draw parts achieve surface finishes ranging from Ra 0.4 µm to Ra 1.6 µm directly from the die, with polished die faces below Ra 0.2 µm producing mirror-quality surfaces in precision applications. How Does Deep Draw Stamping Improve Manufacturing Efficiency? Deep draw stamping improves manufacturing efficiency through automated forming cycles, repeatable tooling geometry, and high stroke rates that eliminate manual fabrication steps from the production sequence. Mechanical presses operating at 15 to 40 strokes per minute produce finished hollow components directly from coil-fed blank stock, reducing operator handling and inter-process transfer time. Progressive die systems integrate blanking, drawing, redrawing, and trimming operations into a single press tool, compressing a 4-stage manual process into a single continuous automated sequence. Hardened tool steel dies that maintain tolerances of ±0.05 mm to ±0.25 mm across millions of cycles eliminate the dimensional variation introduced by manual forming or welded fabrication methods. The combination of high stroke rates, automated material feeding, and near-net-shape output reduces total part cost by 20% to 40% compared to fabricated alternatives, directly improving manufacturing efficiency at production volumes above 10,000 parts per run. Is Deep Draw Stamping Cost-Effective for Large Production Runs? Yes, deep draw stamping is cost-effective for large production runs. Tooling investment for a deep-draw die set ranges from [$10,000 to $100,000], depending on part complexity, tool steel grade, and die configuration, representing a fixed upfront cost that amortizes over the total production volume. The per-unit tooling cost drops below [$1.00] at production volumes above 10,000 parts, making the process economically superior to machining or fabricated alternatives that carry variable cost structures. Automated press cycles operating at 15 to 40 strokes per minute minimize direct labor cost per part, while material utilization rates from 85% to 95% reduce raw material expenditure across the production run. The combination of low per-unit labor cost, high material efficiency, and long tool life (exceeding 500,000 cycles on hardened tool steel dies) makes deep-draw stamping a cost-effective forming method for high-volume hollow-component production. What Are the Applications of Deep Draw Stamping? The applications of deep draw stamping are concentrated in industries that require hollow, single, high-volume components with precise dimensional tolerances and consistent structural integrity. The process is well-suited to manufacturing sectors where part geometry, production volume, and material performance requirements align with the capabilities of punch-and-die forming technology. The applications of deep draw stamping are listed below. Automotive : Deep draw stamping produces fuel tanks, oil filter housings, brake cylinders, airbag canisters, and body panel components at production volumes exceeding 100,000 units per program. Low-carbon steel and aluminum alloys are the primary materials, selected for ductility, weight efficiency, and compliance with automotive structural requirements. Aerospace : Aerospace applications include fuel system housings, hydraulic actuator cylinders, oxygen canister shells, and structural enclosures formed from aluminum alloys, titanium, and nickel superalloys. Tight dimensional tolerances from ±0.05 mm to ±0.10 mm and high strength-to-weight ratios define the forming requirements for aerospace deep-drawn components. Consumer Appliances : Kitchen sinks, washing machine drums, compressor housings, and cookware are produced by deep-draw stamping from stainless steel and aluminum alloys. High surface-finish requirements (Ra 0.4 µm to 1.6 µm) and corrosion resistance drive material selection for deep-drawn appliance components. Electronics : Electronic enclosures, battery casings, heat sink housings, and connector shells are formed by deep-draw stamping from aluminum alloys and copper-based materials. Tight wall-thickness tolerances (±0.05 mm) and electromagnetic shielding requirements define the dimensional specifications for deep-drawn electronic components. Medical Devices : Surgical instrument housings, implant shells, infusion pump casings, and diagnostic device enclosures are produced from 316L stainless steel and commercially pure titanium via deep-draw stamping. Biocompatibility, corrosion resistance, and dimensional precision from ±0.05 mm to ±0.10 mm are the primary material and process requirements for medical deep-drawn components. Industrial Equipment : Hydraulic cylinder bodies, pressure vessel shells, pump housings, and filtration canisters are formed by deep-draw stamping from low-carbon and stainless steel. Wall thickness uniformity achieved through downstream ironing and pressure containment integrity are the critical performance requirements for industrial deep drawn components. How Does Deep Draw Stamping Compare to Metal Spinning? Deep draw stamping compares to metal spinning through fundamental differences in forming mechanics, tooling requirements, production volume suitability, and achievable geometric complexity. Deep draw stamping uses a hardened punch-and-die tool set to plastically deform a flat blank into a hollow shape in a single press stroke, producing parts at rates from 15 to 40 strokes per minute. Metal spinning rotates a flat blank or tube against a mandrel while a roller progressively forms the material into an axisymmetric shape, with cycle times of 1 to 10 minutes per part, depending on geometry and material. Deep draw stamping requires an upfront tooling investment of [$10,000 to $100,000] per die set but delivers per-unit costs below [$1.00] at volumes above 10,000 parts. The metal spinning uses low-cost mandrel tooling of [$500 to $5,000], suited to prototyping and low-volume production. Deep draw stamping produces non-axisymmetric geometries (box shapes, rectangular enclosures) that metal spinning cannot form due to the rotational constraint of the spinning process. The metal spinning offers a cost-effective alternative for axisymmetric components at low-to-medium volumes (below 5,000 parts), while deep draw stamping dominates high-volume production programs requiring tight tolerances and fast cycle rates. How Is Deep Drawing Different from Hydroforming? Deep drawing is different from hydroforming through the mechanism used to deform the blank into the die cavity during the forming operation. Deep drawing relies on a solid mechanical punch that contacts the blank and pushes it through the die opening, generating tensile and compressive stresses via direct tool-to-metal force transfer. Hydroforming replaces the solid punch with pressurized hydraulic fluid, commonly at pressures from 100 MPa to 400 MPa, which acts uniformly across the blank surface to force the material into the die cavity without a contacting punch. The uniform pressure distribution in hydroforming reduces thinning gradients across the part wall, producing uniform wall thickness compared to conventional punch-driven deep drawing. Deep drawing achieves faster cycle rates (15 to 40 strokes per minute) and lower tooling costs, while Hydroforming delivers superior geometric complexity and wall-thickness uniformity for low- to medium-volume applications requiring intricate contours or undercut features. Is Deep Draw Stamping Better for High-Volume Production Than Metal Spinning? Yes, deep draw stamping is better for high-volume production than metal spinning. Mechanical presses in deep-draw stamping operate at 15 to 40 strokes per minute, producing finished parts in seconds, whereas metal spinning requires 1 to 10 minutes per part due to the progressive roller-forming sequence. Deep draw stamping amortizes tooling investment from [$10,000 to $100,000] across production volumes exceeding 10,000 parts, reducing per-unit tooling cost below [$1.00] at high volumes. Metal spinning mandrel tooling costs [$500 to $5,000] per set but incurs higher per-unit labor costs due to the operator-intensive nature of the spinning process at scale. The deep draw stamping delivers lower total cost per part at production volumes above 10,000 parts per run, faster throughput, and tighter dimensional repeatability (±0.05 mm to ±0.25 mm) than metal spinning. What Are the Limitations of Deep Draw Stamping? The limitations of deep draw stamping are tooling costs, geometric constraints, material constraints, and defect risks that define the process's applicability in precision manufacturing. High upfront tooling investment, draw ratio constraints, material ductility requirements, and the risk of wrinkling, tearing, and springback limit the range of parts and production scenarios for which deep draw stamping is the optimal forming choice. Tooling investment ranges from [$10,000 to $100,000] per die set, making low-volume production economically unviable for runs below 5,000 parts. The process requires materials with elongation values above 20% and yield-to-tensile strength ratios below 0.65, excluding brittle or low-ductility alloys from the material selection pool. Draw ratio constraints cap single-stage geometry at an LDR of 2.3, restricting deep or complex parts to multi-stage processing sequences. Understanding the limitations guides engineers toward the appropriate process selection for parts that fall outside the geometric or material capability envelope of deep-draw stamping. Why Are Tooling Costs Higher in Deep Draw Manufacturing? Tooling costs are higher in deep-draw manufacturing because the punches, dies, and blank holders require hardened precision tool steel (D2, H13) machined to tight dimensional tolerances and heat-treated to 58 to 62 HRC before production use. Die cavity geometry must be machined to accuracies of ±0.01 mm to ±0.05 mm using Computer Numerical Control (CNC) grinding and Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) processes, which require specialized equipment and extended machining lead times of 4 to 12 weeks. Tool steel material cost, CNC machining hours, heat treatment, surface coating (TiN, TiCN), and die spotting trials collectively drive tooling investment from [$10,000 to $100,000] per die set, depending on part complexity and die configuration. Multi-stage progressive die sets for parts requiring 3 to 5 draw operations carry tooling costs from [$50,000 to $300,000], significantly increasing the capital commitment before the first production part is formed. The high tooling cost structure makes deep-draw stamping economically viable at production volumes of 5,000 to 10,000 parts, where the fixed tooling cost amortizes to an acceptable per-unit contribution. Can Deep Draw Stamping Produce Complex Geometries in a Single Operation? No, deep draw stamping cannot produce complex geometries in a single operation. Simple cylindrical and shallow box-shaped parts with draw ratios below 1.8 are achievable in a single press stroke without intermediate processing. Parts with draw ratios from 1.8 to 2.3, non-uniform wall profiles, undercut features, or re-entrant geometries require multi-stage progressive drawing sequences, intermediate annealing steps, and secondary trimming or piercing operations to achieve the final geometry. Undercut features and reverse-draft walls are geometrically incompatible with conventional punch-and-die deep drawing in a single operation, requiring secondary forming processes (hydroforming, spinning, or machining) to complete the part geometry. Geometry complexity, draw ratio, and feature configuration collectively determine whether a part requires single-stage or multi-stage deep-draw stamping. events.before: Resources Supplier Shop Tips How Partners With ITAR Registration Earn More How Partners With ITAR Registration Earn More Written by Tricia Contreras 5 min read Published October 19, 2026 ITAR registration gives Xometry Partners access to high-precision, technical manufacturing work. Here's how to register, what it costs, and how to decide if it's worth it for your shop. If you are looking to expand your shop's revenue streams, adding key industry certifications can give you access to high-precision, technical manufacturing work. Certified shops in the Xometry Partner Network earn more on average and access higher-value jobs sooner than non-certified shops. Work requiring certifications generated roughly 3.4 times the annual job value of non-certified work in 2025, while demand for certification-required work grew 56% year over year across the Xometry platform. Among these credentials, International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) registration stands out as one of the most impactful steps manufacturing facilities can take when looking to capture market share in industries that require it, specifically aerospace and defense. “ITAR registration gives Partners access to significantly more aerospace and defense work. A&D is home to many of our top customers, and roughly 90% of those jobs require ITAR compliance, which opens the door to more complex projects,” said Mark Kearney, vice president of quality operations and regulatory at Xometry. Grow Your Shop With Xometry Learn how becoming a Xometry Partner can help your business find profitable work, improve cash flow, and maximize shop efficiency. How to Register for ITAR Before evaluating costs and potential returns, it helps to understand what ITAR registration entails. ITAR registration is mandatory for any US company that manufactures, exports, or brokers defense articles, services, or related data covered by the US Munitions List (USML). The US Department of State's Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) administers ITAR. Registration itself is an administrative filing, not a certification of operational controls. While the registration confirms your business is officially on record with the State Department, complying with ITAR on a day-to-day basis requires additional internal infrastructure, including: Designating an Empowered Official (EO) within your organization to oversee compliance Documenting strict physical and digital access controls Implementing ongoing compliance training for employees Maintaining rigorous recordkeeping standards for a minimum of five years Once your shop is prepared to initiate the administrative filing, follow these steps to complete the process: 1. Determine Eligibility: Confirm that your facility manufactures, exports, or brokers defense items or technical data listed on the USML. 2. Access the DECCS Portal: Create an account in the Defense Export Control and Compliance System (DECCS) , the electronic portal administered by the DDTC for all registration filings. 3. Submit Form DS-2032: Complete and submit Form DS-2032 (Statement of Registration), outlining your corporate structure, facility locations, and business activities. 4. Pay the Registration Fee: Pay the annual fee corresponding to your registration tier via the DECCS online payment system. 5. Await Approval and Maintain Annual Renewal: Once reviewed and approved by the DDTC, you will receive your official ITAR registration letter. Registration must be renewed annually to remain active. What ITAR Registration Costs The DDTC has a fee schedule for manufacturers and exporters based on which tier they fall into. Tier 1 ($3,000 / year): Applies to new registrants and registrants that do not export. Qualifying small businesses can receive a reduced rate of $2,500 per year if they can prove that $3,000 was 1% or more of their total revenue for the last calendar year. Tier 2 ($4,000 / year): Applies to registrants that submitted between one and five favorable export licenses or determinations during the preceding 12-month period. Tier 3 ($4,000 base + $1,100 per determination beyond five): Designed for high-volume defense exporters that require more than five favorable determinations per year. Why Registered Partners Earn More While the initial fee required for ITAR registration is a direct overhead expense, the financial benefits of registration extend to both job-level margins and your shop’s long-term enterprise value. From a corporate valuation perspective, defense contractors with ITAR registration and CMMC 2.0 certification typically sell for 7-10x EBITDA, compared to a selling price of 5-7x EBITDA for non-compliant businesses, according to CT Acquisitions . Operationally, Tier-1 contractors prefer to send work to compliant facilities. Subcontracted defense work requires prime buyers to verify ITAR compliance separately for each unregistered supplier in their supply chain, which creates a strong preference for partnering directly with shops that already hold active registration. Aerospace and defense buyers work with Xometry because it allows them to streamline sourcing by sending all their orders through the Xometry platform to be matched with certified Partners. On the Xometry platform, quality and compliance credentials directly unlock high-value jobs for these prime buyers. ITAR-registered Partners and Partners holding certifications such as ISO 9001:2015, AS9100D, ISO 13485:2016, IATF 16949:2016, CMMC Level 2, or JCP earn more on average and access higher-value jobs sooner. Currently, Xometry has about 500 ITAR-registered Partners across its network, collectively processing approximately 2,000 ITAR-controlled jobs each month — and demand for this type of certification-required work is growing. Deciding If It's Worth It for Your Shop Deciding whether to register comes down to weighing the $2,500 to $3,000 entry cost against your shop's long-term commercial goals. If your facility aims to stay focused purely on commercial prototype parts or non-sensitive industrial components, standard certifications like ISO 9001 may suffice. However, if your strategic plan includes securing steady, higher-margin defense work, capturing a share of the growing number of ITAR jobs being ordered through Xometry, or building enterprise value for a future sale, ITAR registration can offer a major return on investment. Join the Xometry Partner Network Ready to grow your shop's revenue and access high-value work for top-tier customers? Learn more about how to join the Xometry Partner Network and upload your active facility certifications today. Tricia Contreras Tricia is a Senior Content Strategist at Xometry. Qualifying small businesses can receive a reduced rate of $2,500 per year if they can prove that $3,000 was 1% or more of their total revenue for the last calendar year. Tier 2 ($4,000 / year): Applies to registrants that submitted between one and five favorable export licenses or determinations during the preceding 12-month period. Tier 3 ($4,000 base + $1,100 per determination beyond five): Designed for high-volume defense exporters that require more than five favorable determinations per year. Why Registered Partners Earn More While the initial fee required for ITAR registration is a direct overhead expense, the financial benefits of registration extend to both job-level margins and your shop’s long-term enterprise value. From a corporate valuation perspective, defense contractors with ITAR registration and CMMC 2.0 certification typically sell for 7-10x EBITDA, compared to a selling price of 5-7x EBITDA for non-compliant businesses, according to CT Acquisitions . Operationally, Tier-1 contractors prefer to send work to compliant facilities. Subcontracted defense work requires prime buyers to verify ITAR compliance separately for each unregistered supplier in their supply chain, which creates a strong preference for partnering directly with shops that already hold active registration. Aerospace and defense buyers work with Xometry because it allows them to streamline sourcing by sending all their orders through the Xometry platform to be matched with certified Partners. On the Xometry platform, quality and compliance credentials directly unlock high-value jobs for these prime buyers. ITAR-registered Partners and Partners holding certifications such as ISO 9001:2015, AS9100D, ISO 13485:2016, IATF 16949:2016, CMMC Level 2, or JCP earn more on average and access higher-value jobs sooner. Currently, Xometry has about 500 ITAR-registered Partners across its network, collectively processing approximately 2,000 ITAR-controlled jobs each month — and demand for this type of certification-required work is growing. Deciding If It's Worth It for Your Shop Deciding whether to register comes down to weighing the $2,500 to $3,000 entry cost against your shop's long-term commercial goals. If your facility aims to stay focused purely on commercial prototype parts or non-sensitive industrial components, standard certifications like ISO 9001 may suffice. However, if your strategic plan includes securing steady, higher-margin defense work, capturing a share of the growing number of ITAR jobs being ordered through Xometry, or building enterprise value for a future sale, ITAR registration can offer a major return on investment. Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. PCBWay Store NewArrival Product - ESP32-C5 Mini Dual-band Development Board Clock Circuit Design Guidelines for PCB Layout BGA Assembly Capabilities When it comes to BGA assembly, let's first understand what BGA is. BGAs (Ball Grid Arrays) are a type of IC package where the pins are placed in the form of solder balls. Compared to traditional packaging technologies such as DIP (Dual In-line Package) or QFP (Quad Flat Package), BGA employs a higher-density pin layout. With technological advancements, there is an increasing demand in PCB design for complex and small-sized chips. These chips enable higher integration and functionality within smaller spaces. Hence, there is a need for a packaging method that can accommodate these chips with higher I/O density while maintaining cost-effectiveness. BGA (Ball Grid Array) is precisely such a packaging method that meets these requirements. What is BGA Assembly? BGA assembly refers to the process of mounting a Ball Grid Array (BGA) onto a PCB using the reflow soldering technique. BGA is a surface-mounted component that utilizes an array of solder balls for electrical interconnection. As the circuit board passes through a solder reflow oven, these solder balls melt, forming electrical connections. Steps of BGA Assembly The BGA assembly process typically involves the following steps: PCB Preparation: The PCB is prepared by applying solder paste to the pads where the BGA will be mounted. The solder paste is a mixture of solder alloy particles and flux, which helps with the soldering process. Placement of BGAs: The BGAs, which consist of the integrated circuit chip with solder balls on the bottom, are placed onto the prepared PCB. This is typically done using automated pick-and-place machines or other assembly equipment. Reflow Soldering: The assembled PCB with the placed BGAs is then passed through a reflow oven. The reflow oven heats the PCB to a specific temperature that melts the solder paste, causing the solder balls of the BGAs to reflow and establish electrical connections with the PCB pads. Cooling and Inspection: After the solder reflow process, the PCB is cooled down to solidify the solder joints. It is then inspected for any defects, such as misalignment, shorts, or open connections. Automated optical inspection (AOI) or X-ray inspection may be used for this purpose. Secondary Processes: Depending on the specific requirements, additional processes such as cleaning, testing, and conformal coating may be performed after BGA assembly to ensure the reliability and quality of the finished product. Advantages of BGA Assembly Small footprint BGA packaging consists of the chip, interconnects, a thin substrate, and an encapsulation cover. There are few exposed components and the package has a minimal number of pins. The overall height of the chip on the PCB can be as low as 1.2 millimeters. Robustness BGA packaging is highly robust. Unlike QFP with a 20mil pitch, BGA does not have pins that can bend or break. Generally, BGA removal requires the use of a BGA rework station at high temperatures. Lower parasitic inductance and capacitance With short pins and low assembly height, BGA packaging exhibits low parasitic inductance and capacitance, resulting in excellent electrical performance. Increased storage space Compared to other packaging types, BGA packaging has only one-third of the volume and approximately 1.2 times the chip area. Memory and operational products using BGA packaging can achieve more than a 2.1-fold increase in storage capacity and operational speed. High stability Due to the direct extension of pins from the center of the chip in BGA packaging, the transmission paths for various signals are effectively shortened, reducing signal attenuation and improving response speed and anti-interference capabilities. This enhances the stability of the product. Good heat dissipation BGA offers excellent heat dissipation performance, with the chip temperature approaching the ambient temperature during operation. Convenient for rework The pins of BGA packaging are neatly arranged on the bottom, making it easy to locate damaged areas for removal. This facilitates the rework of BGA chips. Avoidance of wiring chaos BGA packaging allows for placing many power and ground pins in the center, with I/O pins positioned on the periphery. Pre-routing can be done on the BGA substrate, avoiding chaotic wiring of I/O pins. PCBWay BGA Assembly Capabilities PCBWay is a globally renowned manufacturer for PCB fabrication and PCB assembly. Board Shape We can assemble boards in Rectangular, Circular and any Odd Shapes. PCBWay Store NewArrival Product - ESP32-C5 Mini Dual-band Development Board Clock Circuit Design Guidelines for PCB Layout SMT Assembly Capabilities What is SMT Assembly? SMT, which stands for Surface Mount Technology, is a method of directly mounting electronic components onto the surface of a PCB. This method is commonly used for installing Surface Mount Devices (SMDs), which have smaller pins or are pinless in structure. Compared to traditional through-hole technology, SMT provides higher levels of automated manufacturing capabilities, reduces costs, and improves quality. Additionally, SMT allows for the installation of more components on a limited PCB board area. Through-hole technology is typically used for components such as large transformers and high-power heat-dissipating semiconductors that are not suitable for surface mounting. SMT components have smaller leads or no leads at all, and common structures include short pins or leads, flat contacts, and Ball Grid Arrays (BGAs). PCBWay SMT Assembly Capability Overview We have the capabilities to assemble SMT prototype PCBs in small production runs with manual and/or automated SMT production processes, including single- or double-sided component insertions. Our production facilities can assemble the following SMT types: Ball Grid Array (BGA) Ultra-Fine Ball Grid Array (uBGA) Quad Flat Pack No-Lead (QFN) Quad Flat Package (QFP) Small Outline Integrated Circuit (SOIC) Plastic Leaded Chip Carrier (PLCC) Package-On-Package (PoP) Small Chip Packages (0.2mm pitch ) Main SMT Machines in PCBWay Automatic Solder Paste Printer Reflow Soldering Machine Pick & Place Machine Inspection equipment (3D SPI machine, online AOI machine, offline AOI machine, X-Ray machine) SMT Manufacturing Process SMT Process Flow Chart PCB, SMC, Stencil Preparation and Examination Prepare the PCB, surface-mount components, and stencil, and inspect them for any defects. Solder Paste Printing The solder paste screen printing machine used for SMT is required to print solder paste onto the PCB before surface-mount components undergo reflow soldering. 3D Solder Paste Inspection The solder paste printing process is one of the most critical stages in SMT assembly. The earlier the defects are identified, the lower the cost of correcting them. To ensure defect-free solder paste deposition in the required quantity, it is recommended to perform a comprehensive inspection of each printed PCB before commencing component placement. 3D solder paste inspection not only checks the coverage area and short circuits of the solder paste but also accurately measures the shape and volume of the solder deposits. On the other hand, 2D solder paste inspection cannot assess the volume or shape of the solder deposition. Pick & Place The SMT pick and place machine is one of the most crucial equipments in surface mount technology. It is also referred to as the pick-and-place robot. Prior to soldering, it picks up SMDs and places them onto the PCB. Reflow Soldering Reflow Oven: After the surface mount components are placed, the PCB is sent into the reflow oven. Preheat Zone: The first zone in the reflow oven is the preheat zone, where the temperature of the PCB and all components gradually increases simultaneously. The heating rate in this stage is 1.0°C-2.0°C per second until it reaches 140°C-160°C. Soaking Zone: The PCB remains at a temperature of 140°C-160°C for a soaking period of 60-90 seconds. Reflow Zone: The circuit board then enters a peak temperature zone where the temperature rises at a rate of 1.0°C-2.0°C per second until it reaches a peak of 210°C-230°C. This melts the solder in the solder paste, bonding the component leads to the solder pads on the PCB. The surface tension of the molten solder helps to hold the components in place. Cooling Zone: In the cooling zone, the heated PCB and components gradually cool down, allowing the solder joints to solidify and stabilize. The cooling process is critical for the formation of solder joints and securing the components. It helps ensure the reliability and mechanical strength of the solder joints. If the circuit board is double-sided, the printing, placement, and reflow process can be repeated using solder paste or adhesive to secure the components in place. AOI Machine Inspection After the soldering process, professional quality inspectors will perform AOI on the circuit boards to check for any defects before the products are stored in the warehouse. Get a quote Rapid Prototyping CNC Machining CNC Milling Overview Features Processes Materials Finishes Tolerances Industries Reviews Resources Quote Now! Overview: How CNC Milling works? The Basics Of CNC Mills CNC mills are automated cutting machines using a rotating spindle-head to cut away unwanted material. CNC milling machines come in a variety of sizes and different axis configurations. They are mainly utilized to cut harder metals but can work with workpiece materials ranging from plastic and aluminum to stainless steel and titanium. How Does CNC Milling Work? Overview: What is CNC Turning? The Basics Of CNC Lathes CNC turning machines are able to provide low cost parts for simple cylindrical geometries. Live tooling is available for more complex geometries and is assessed on a case by case basis. How CNC Turning Works Use a single-point cutting tools to remove material from the rotating workpiece. In CNC turning, the CNC machine, typically a lathe or turning machine, feeds the cutting tool in a linear motion along the surface of the rotating workpiece, removing material around the circumference until the desired diameter is achieved. Most CNC lathes consist of two axis, X and Z. Common Applications functional prototypes and end-use parts parts with cylindrical features parts with axial and radial holes, flats, grooves, and slots Types Of CNC Turning There are many types of CNC turning operations for CNC lathe services can be performed on a live tooling lathe in CNC turning factory, including Hard turning, Parting, Facing, Boring, Reaming, Taper turning, Drilling, Knurling, Threading, Grooving, etc., comes in varying tools, cost and set-up time. 1.Tapered turning: produce a cylindrical part of which diameter decrease from one end to another. 2.Hard turning: suited for materials with a Rockwell C hardness greater than 45, typically performed after heat treated. 3.Spherical generation: create a spherical finished surface, turning around fixed rotary axis. 4.Facing: a turning operation in which the workpiece is machined to its center. 5.Parting: create deep grooves that remove a completed or part-complete component from its parent stock. 6.Grooving: similar to parting, but only cut to a specific depth from outside or inside of workpiece. 7.Drilling: remove materials to drill holes from the inside of a workpiece with drill bits held stationary in the tail stock or tool turret of the lathe. Boring: enlarge or smooth an existing hole. 8.Knurling: cut serrated pattern onto the surface of workpiece with knurling tool, to change or enhance visual effect or hand grip. 9.Reaming: remove a small volume of materials from a drilled hole, for highly accurate diameters. 10.Threading: turn standard and non-standard screw threads, generally means single-point threading. 11.Polygonal turning: non-circular forms machining operation without interrupting the rotation of the raw material. Features of CNC Machining Advantages Rapid Turnaround Using the latest CNC machines, PCBWay produces highly accurate, quick turn parts in as fast as 2 day. We also instantly quote CNC machined parts, cutting days off of your RFQ process. High Precision Tolerances Offers high-precision tolerances ranging from +/-0.001″ – 0.005″, depending on customer specs. We are the experts in making parts that are truly custom and ready to use. Scalability CNC Machining is perfect for prototyping and production production parts. PCBWay's massive scale can help you scale up from testing phase to production runs of 100,000 parts of more. Custom Surface Finishes Suitable for many different kinds of substrates, make your parts just the same as real products. Material Selection Choose from over 50 metal and plastic materials. CNC Machining offers a wide variety of certified materials. Cost Saving Low investment in tooling and preparation costs, economical for parts with simple structure. Drawbacks Structure Limits Interlocking and hollowed structure is difficult to be machined with CNC. Scale Effect The unit cost and lead time will not be reduced as much as injection molded parts. Our standard surface finishes Here is a list of standard surface finishes. For custom surface finishes such as electroplating or polishing, please contact 3dcnc@pcbway.com. As-Milled The finish option with the quickest turnaround. Parts are left with visible tool marks and potentially sharp edges and burrs, which can be removed upon request. Surface finish is comparable to 125 uin Ra finish. Bead Blast Abrasive blasting, more commonly known as sandblasting, is the operation of forcibly propelling a stream of abrasive material against a surface under high pressure to smooth a rough surface, roughen a smooth surface, shape a surface or remove surface contaminants. Requirement Specification Grit #120 Color Uniform matte of raw material color Part masking Indicate masking requirements in technical drawing Anodized (Type II Or Type III) Type II creates a corrosion-resistant finish. Parts can be anodized in different colors—clear, black, red, and gold are most common—and is usually associated with aluminum. Type III is thicker and creates a wear-resistant layer in addition to the corrosion resistance seen with Type II. Requirement Specification Grit #120 Color Uniform matte of raw material color Part masking Indicate masking requirements in technical drawing Bead Blasting + Anodizing color or clear (type II) Type II anodizing is mainly used to produce parts with a uniform, aesthetically pleasing surface and provides good corrosion and limited wear resistance. Parts are bead blasted to #120 grit prior to anodizing. Requirement Specification Thickness 8 - 12 μm (clear), 4 - 8 μm (color) Color Black, clear or any RAL code or Pantone number Part masking Indicate masking requirements in technical drawing Powder Coat This is a process where powdered paint is sprayed onto a part which is then baked in an oven. This creates a strong, wear- and corrosion-resistant layer that is more durable than standard painting methods. A wide variety of colors are available to create the desired aesthetic. Requirement Specification Thickness 18 - 72μm Color Black or any RAL code or Pantone number. Part masking Indicate masking requirements in technical drawing. Electropolished Electropolishing is an electrochemical process used to polish, passivate and deburr metal parts. It is useful to reduce surface roughness. Requirement Specification Color Natural metal color. Part masking Indicate masking requirements in technical drawing. Brushed Brushed or dull polished metal is metal with a unidirectional satin finish. It is produced by polishing the metal with a 120–180 grit belt or wheel then softening with an 80–120 grit greaseless compound or a medium non-woven abrasive belt or pad. Commonly brushed metals include stainless steel, aluminium and nickel. Boring: enlarge or smooth an existing hole. 8.Knurling: cut serrated pattern onto the surface of workpiece with knurling tool, to change or enhance visual effect or hand grip. 9.Reaming: remove a small volume of materials from a drilled hole, for highly accurate diameters. 10.Threading: turn standard and non-standard screw threads, generally means single-point threading. 11.Polygonal turning: non-circular forms machining operation without interrupting the rotation of the raw material.
